content: This cross-sectional study investigated the acceptability of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among men who have sex with men (MSM) in Shenyang, China. The study aimed to identify demographic and behavioral predictors of the intention to use PrEP, which could help in selecting participants for clinical trials. In 2011, 274 MSM were recruited through snowball sampling at voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) centers within the gay community in Shenyang. After a brief introduction to the results of the Truvada clinical trial by trained staff, interviewer-assisted questionnaires were used to collect data on demographics, behaviors, and attitudes toward using Truvada as a daily HIV prevention method. All participants were tested for HIV and syphilis. The study found that PrEP acceptability among Chinese MSM was associated with awareness of PrEP and family support. Future efforts to enroll participants in PrEP trials and promote oral PrEP should focus on education about the medication and increasing family support for participants. A separate study examined factors associated with PrEP and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) use among young MSM who use the social networking app GRINDR in Los Angeles, California. Young MSM contribute disproportionately to new and existing HIV infections in the United States. Combination HIV prevention strategies, including biomedical interventions like PrEP, may reduce HIV infections in this group. Using GRINDR, 375 young MSM were recruited through random venue-date-time sampling. Participants completed a computer-assisted self-interview (CASI) survey. The study revealed that 41% of participants reported inconsistent condom use, and 20% of their sexual partners were either HIV-positive or of unknown serostatus. Despite the demonstrated efficacy of PrEP in MSM, uptake of PrEP and PEP remains limited, particularly among Latino MSM. Social networking applications like GRINDR may serve as effective tools for recruiting participants for prevention interventions and delivering educational messages. A review of previous studies highlighted the need for healthcare providers to be engaged in implementing PrEP. While randomized controlled trials have shown that PrEP can reduce HIV incidence among at-risk populations, including MSM and serodiscordant couples, its real-world effectiveness depends on clinical monitoring and high medication adherence. Many healthcare providers lack sufficient knowledge or express reservations about prescribing PrEP. Training and decision-support interventions for providers are essential to optimize PrEP implementation. Cost-effectiveness studies have shown that PrEP can be a cost-effective HIV prevention strategy in high-risk populations, such as MSM with an HIV incidence of at least 2% in the United States and young women in South Africa. However, the cost-effectiveness of PrEP depends on factors such as medication cost, adherence, and program coverage. Delivering PrEP to key populations at the highest risk of HIV exposure appears to be the most cost-effective strategy. Mathematical modeling studies have demonstrated that the epidemiological impact of PrEP is influenced by program characteristics, such as coverage, prioritization strategies, and adherence behavior. While PrEP can avert new infections and save lives, it will not eliminate HIV transmission on its own due to incomplete effectiveness, adherence challenges, and high program costs. Strategic implementation of PrEP, particularly among vulnerable populations, could be a cost-effective addition to existing HIV prevention programs. In summary, while PrEP has shown promise as an effective HIV prevention tool, its implementation faces challenges related to awareness, adherence, provider engagement, and cost. Further research is needed to address these barriers and optimize the delivery of PrEP as part of comprehensive HIV prevention strategies.
